blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A map service draws a map by splitting each tile into four quarter tiles; a tile of 256 px or less is drawn directly. Each larger tile submits its four quarters to the same Executors.newFixedThreadPool(32) and calls get() on their Futures. City maps come out; a country map never finishes, and the machine's CPUs sit idle. Which change lets every map finish?

options.text: Grow the fixed pool to 512 threads, since the country map then has a free thread for each tile that waits
options.says: every tile that splits holds a thread while it waits, and a larger map has more such tiles; a bigger pool only moves the map size at which it hangs

options.text: Make each tile a RecursiveTask in a ForkJoinPool that forks and joins its quarters, since a worker waiting in join() runs queued tasks
options.says: a ForkJoinPool worker that joins a task that isn't done looks for queued work and runs it, so the quarters it waits for get run

options.text: Grow the fixed pool with a second one for the quarters, since tiles that wait then no longer hold the threads that draw
options.says: the quarters split and wait too, so the second pool fills with waiting quarters the same way

options.text: Make each tile a RecursiveTask in a ForkJoinPool that forks and joins its quarters, since the pool adds a thread for each tile that waits
options.says: join() runs the awaited task or helps the worker that took it; the pool starts a spare thread only when a joining worker has nothing to run, not one per waiting task, and the page's ForkJoinPool(8) finished 8 million rows

origin.section: A Task That Waits for Its Subtasks Deadlocks an Ordinary Pool; ForkJoinPool's join() Keeps Working

questions.stem: A RecursiveTask counts words in a list of documents and stops splitting at 5,000 documents. Its compute() ends with `left.fork(); long a = left.join(); long b = right.compute(); return a + b;`. On a ForkJoinPool of 12 the count is right, but the job takes 9 seconds, the same as a plain loop. What explains it?

options.text: Each task waits for its left half before it starts its right half, so the two halves of a split never run side by side
options.says: joining before computing makes each level sequential; the swapped order runs at one thread's speed

options.text: Each task waits for its left half in a parked thread, so the pool soon has no worker left that could run anything
options.says: join() looks for queued work before it parks, and the pool still finishes; the problem is the order, not lost workers

options.text: The leaves of 5,000 documents are too small, so creating and queueing tasks costs more than counting the words in them
options.says: 5,000 documents is a lot of work per task; a task's cost matters only when a leaf does very little

options.text: The call to fork() runs the left half on the current thread, so no other worker is ever handed a task to run
options.says: fork() queues the task and returns at once; other workers can steal it

origin.section: Fork One Half, Compute the Other, Then Join

questions.stem: A batch job totals a risk score over 50 million prices, a few dozen nanoseconds of arithmetic per price, with a RecursiveTask that splits until a range holds two prices or fewer, on a ForkJoinPool of 16. It is slower than a plain loop on one thread. Which change makes it faster than the loop?

options.text: Raise the split point to 20,000 prices, since each task then does far more work than it costs to create and queue
options.says: with a task per one or two values the task overhead exceeds the work; a larger threshold leaves a few thousand tasks that still keep every worker busy

options.text: Raise the split point to 50 million prices, since one task then skips the cost of creating and queueing the others
options.says: one task runs on one thread, so it is no faster than the plain loop

options.text: Grow the pool to 64 workers, since more workers take the many small tasks off the queues sooner
options.says: the cost is in creating and queueing tens of millions of tasks, which more workers don't remove

options.text: Move the tasks to a fixed thread pool, since its tasks are cheaper to create and queue than fork/join tasks
options.says: a task that waits for its subtasks deadlocks a fixed pool once the waiting tasks hold every thread

origin.section: The Threshold Decides Whether Splitting Pays

questions.stem: An order service prices carts with CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(...) and no executor; pricing takes 5 ms. A new reporting endpoint runs orders.parallelStream().map(o -> invoiceClient.fetch(o.id())), where fetch() is an HTTP call of about 400 ms. While a report runs, pricing a cart takes over a second. What is the cause?

options.text: Both use the JVM's common pool, so pricing tasks queue behind workers that are inside fetch() calls
options.says: parallel streams and supplyAsync without an executor share the common pool, and workers asleep in HTTP calls run nothing else

options.text: Both use the JVM's common pool, so the report's fetch() calls use up the CPU time that pricing needs
options.says: the workers are asleep waiting for HTTP answers, not computing; the pricing tasks lack threads, not CPU

options.text: The parallel stream starts a thread per order, so the operating system has too many threads to schedule pricing in time
options.says: a parallel stream starts no threads of its own; it runs in the common pool and on its caller

options.text: The parallel stream starts a thread per order, so the HTTP client's connections run out before pricing gets one
options.says: a parallel stream starts no threads of its own, and pricing doesn't use the HTTP client; it waits for a common-pool worker

origin.section: The Common Pool Is Shared, So Blocking in It Delays Work You Didn't Write

concepts: In a ForkJoinPool, fork() queues a task on the current worker's queue, join() runs the awaited task or helps the worker that took it before it parks, and idle workers steal tasks from other workers' queues.

A task that submits its subtasks to a fixed pool and waits for them holds a thread while it waits, so a deep enough split leaves every thread waiting and the job never finishes; a bigger pool only moves the size at which it hangs.
